description: A team of software engineers and data enthusiasts turning NASA open data into robust, mission-ready tools. We focus on clean architecture, efficient algorithms, and practical solutions to tackle critical space and Earth science challenges.
summary:
MoonSight is an interactive tool for comparing landing scenarios near the Moon’s south pole. It helps users explore when the Sun and Earth are visible above the local horizon and understand how surrounding terrain changes those visibility windows.

MoonSight combines NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides with lunar elevation data from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA). Users can compare landing sites and time periods, inspect visibility timelines, and visualize the terrain obstruction behind each result.

In a Connecting Ridge example from January 7–14, 2027 UTC, estimated Earth-center visibility changes from 40.76% above a geometric horizon to 28.31% above the modeled terrain horizon. MoonSight turns this difference into an intuitive visual explanation of why local terrain matters for lunar mission planning.

The project is designed for exploration, education, and early comparison of mission scenarios. It does not certify landing-site safety, calculate actual solar-panel power, guarantee radio communication, or replace mission-grade engineering analysis.

Video demonstration:
https://moonsight-gameoverteam.vercel.app/media/lunawindow-demo.mp4

Source code, methodology, NASA data references, and reproducibility notes:
https://github.com/MironNikanchuk/nasaspace2026
details:
At the Moon’s south pole, the Sun and Earth can remain close to the horizon. Mountains and ridges can block them, changing the periods when a site receives sunlight or has a potential direct line of sight to Earth.

MoonSight makes these conditions easier to explore. A user can select two landing scenarios, compare their Sun and Earth visibility timelines, and inspect an interactive horizon view. Where terrain profiles are available, the user can compare a geometric horizon with a modeled terrain horizon and see why a body becomes obscured.

For example, at Connecting Ridge from January 7 to January 14, 2027, the Earth’s center is visible above the geometric horizon for 40.76% of the interval. With the modeled terrain horizon, it is visible for 28.31%. This illustrates why local terrain matters when comparing scenarios.

MoonSight uses NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides for apparent Sun and Earth positions and terrain profiles derived from NASA LRO LOLA elevation data. Candidate site coordinates are based on the NASA Lunar Surface Data Book. The application combines a Python/FastAPI calculation backend with a Next.js interactive frontend and 3D visualizations.

The project is designed for exploration, education, and early comparison of scenarios. It estimates visibility of the centers of the Sun and Earth; it does not calculate actual solar-panel power, guarantee radio communication, or certify landing-site safety. Results depend on the selected period, terrain coverage, resolution, and model assumptions.

We hope MoonSight makes lunar mission-planning concepts easier to investigate for students, educators, the public, and people exploring early mission scenarios.
